core: Working definition of a liability: an obligation to pay or deliver something in the future, created by a past business activity
Common liability types: accounts payable, loans (notes payable), wages payable, taxes payable (plus unearned revenue as an advance-payment liability)
Current vs long-term liabilities: the one-year (or operating-cycle) rule
Liabilities in the accounting equation: right side, assets = liabilities + equity (equation mechanics belong to the sibling topic)
How liabilities arise: buying on credit, borrowing, accruing obligations
Liabilities vs expenses: owed amounts vs costs incurred
Honest framing: liabilities fund growth and must be managed, not feared
supporting: Unearned revenue as a liability (advance payment for undelivered goods or services)
Classified balance sheet lists current liabilities before noncurrent
Current portion of a long-term loan is split into current vs long-term
Operating cycle convention as the alternative delimiter
outOfScope: Journal entries, GAAP vs IFRS specifics, ratio analysis

claims.claim: A liability is an obligation to pay money or deliver assets or services in the future, created by a past business activity or transaction.
Liabilities sit on the right side of the accounting equation, assets = liabilities + equity, and the equation treats liabilities and equity as the two sources that fund a company's assets.
Accounts payable are amounts owed to suppliers for goods or services purchased on credit.
Loans and notes payable are formal borrowing arrangements in which the business promises to repay borrowed funds; loans, notes, bonds, and mortgages are all forms of debt that must be repaid.
Wages (salaries) payable are amounts employees have earned that the business has not yet paid.
Taxes payable are taxes the business has incurred or collected but not yet remitted, such as income tax payable and sales tax.
Current liabilities are due within one year, or within the operating cycle if that is longer; long-term (noncurrent) liabilities are due in a later period.
The portion of a long-term loan due within the current year is classified as a current liability, and the rest as long-term.
Current liabilities are reported on the classified balance sheet, listed before noncurrent liabilities, and lenders watch them to judge a company's short-term cash needs.
Unearned revenue is a customer's advance payment for a product or service the company has not yet provided, and is therefore a liability until the product or service is delivered.
Liabilities commonly arise three ways: buying on credit (accounts payable), borrowing (notes payable), and accruing obligations such as wages and taxes owed.
An expense is a cost incurred; a liability is an amount owed. An incurred-but-unpaid cost is both an expense and a liability until it is settled.

Borrowing is a normal funding source for business growth: companies borrow funds, creating liabilities, as one of the two sources of assets alongside equity; the risk is unmanaged debt, not debt itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The one-year cutoff for current liabilities is a convention, not a fixed rule.
positions: OpenStax: current liabilities are due within the company's standard operating period, typically a year, with exceptions longer or shorter
CFI: current liabilities are due within one year, or within one business cycle if the cycle is longer
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach the one-year rule with the operating-cycle caveat; both sources agree the delimiter is the longer of the year or the operating cycle.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is debt good or bad for a business?
positions: Debt funds operations and growth and is a normal financing source per the accounting equation
Excessive or unmanaged debt threatens solvency (burn-rate discussion in OpenStax 12.1)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Frame liabilities as neutral and normal — they must be managed. Both positions are preserved in the lesson's honest-framing section.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Section 12.1: Identify and Describe Current Liabilities
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports: liabilities require a future disbursement of assets or services resulting from a prior business activity or transaction; current liability is a debt or obligation due within the standard operating period, typically a year; noncurrent liabilities are long-term obligations due in a subsequent period; current liabilities are reported on the classified balance sheet before noncurrent; common current liabilities include accounts payable (obligations owed to suppliers after purchasing on credit), salaries payable, taxes payable, unearned revenues (advance payment for a product or service yet to be provided, e.g., gift cards and deposits for services), and the current portion of a note payable; accounts payable agreements usually do not include interest, unlike notes payable; accrued interest payable can be a current liability; burn rate and cash-needs relevance. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Current Liabilities (CFI)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports: current liabilities are financial obligations due and payable within a year (or one business cycle if longer); a liability arises when a company enters a transaction that creates an expectation of a future outflow of cash or other economic resources; accounts payable arise from a purchase not yet fully paid off or recurring credit terms with suppliers; other categories include accrued expenses, short-term notes payable, current portion of long-term notes payable, and income tax payable; a current liability appears on the balance sheet's liability side; the distinction between accrued expenses and accounts payable. Facts restated in original prose.
